speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: asked the Minister for National Development given that HDB announced housing plans for Gillman Barracks and Sunset Way on the same day consultation opened (a) which parameters remain open to change, including footprint, yield, retained areas, heritage and mitigation; (b) whether site clearance or tender awards will await feedback; and (c) whether HDB will publish its response before approving final plans or tenders.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: asked the Minister for National Development in light of the recent announcement on Maju Forest (a) how has the Government's approach to balancing public housing needs with the conservation of ecologically significant forests and heat resilience evolved over the past five years; and (b) whether alternative sites, redevelopment opportunities or higher-yield development options are systematically evaluated before such locations are selected.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: asked the Minister for National Development with regard to proposed housing developments on former forested sites (a) what criteria are used to determine whether retained forest areas are sufficiently large and connected to remain ecologically functional over the long term; and (b) how is the effectiveness of wildlife corridors subsequently monitored.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: asked the Minister for National Development in light of the possible development at Maju Forest, whether the concerns and recommendations of the nature and conservation groups on preserving greenery, flora and fauna can be adopted.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: asked the Minister for National Development (a) how were findings from the Gillman Barracks Environmental and Heritage Impact Assessments weighed against housing needs; (b) whether alternative sites were considered; and (c) what resident engagement was conducted prior to the redevelopment announcement, including whether closed-door discussions were held and how participants were selected.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: asked the Minister for National Development (a) how are findings from the Maju Forest Environmental Impact Assessment taken into account in ongoing considerations for housing at Sunset Way; (b) whether alternative sites can be considered; and (c) what measures are being considered to ensure any retained ecological corridor minimises edge effects and supports wildlife movement.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: asked the Minister for National Development (a) what microclimate or urban heat-island modelling was conducted to assess the localised temperature impact of clearing forest cover at Maju Forest and Gillman Barracks; and (b) what will be the projected impact on surrounding residential areas.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: asked the Minister for National Development regarding the Gillman Barracks redevelopment (a) what measures will be taken to ensure the preservation of its secondary hill forest and heritage buildings; (b) whether alternative brownfield sites were considered to minimise ecological impact; and (c) how public feedback from the environmental and heritage impact assessments will be incorporated into the final master plan.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen
text: asked the Minister for National Development what planning criteria does the Ministry use to determine that brownfield and other previously developed sites are insufficient before greenfield sites are selected for residential development.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen
text: asked the Minister for National Development whether the Ministry will further enhance the public accessibility of Environmental Impact Assessments by providing plain-language summaries of key findings and clearer explanations of how public feedback has informed planning decisions.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee
text: asked the Minister for National Development (a) how was public feedback gathered for the redevelopment of Maju Forest and Gillman Barracks; and (b) what other sites are being studied over the next five years for similar possible redevelopment for housing or other uses that may substantially affect existing heritage or natural areas.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
text: asked the Minister for National Development in light of the recent announcement on Maju Forest (a) whether future Master Plans will refrain from zoning forested greenfield sites for development where feasible, especially where the forested sites are of ecological significance, and prioritise the redevelopment and intensifying land use on existing brownfield sites; and (b) if not, why not.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Government will continue to engage stakeholders, to take in views and feedback before deciding how we will carry out the development of both sites.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This could involve adjustments to the development layout and the amount of greenery and heritage to conserve.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I will then explain how these principles apply to Sunset Way and Gillman Barracks.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We also want Singaporeans and our future generations to have access to affordable public housing.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We want hospitals, schools, and places where we can work and earn a good living.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We want roads and public transport so we can get around.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We also need land for defence, essential infrastructure and coastal protection.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And I wish we had an abundance of land, so we can provide all of these without having to make trade-offs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Our choices are narrower than those faced by larger countries.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We thus have to make the best use of our limited land.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: That is why we plan decades ahead, to meet Singaporeans' needs today while keeping enough options open for future generations.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Housing is one of our most pressing needs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Some asked why housing demand continues to grow even though our total fertility rate (TFR) is lower than before.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Current low TFR figures reflect the smaller number of babies born in recent years.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But Singaporeans who are buying Housing and Development Board (HDB) homes today and in the near future were born decades ago when our birth rates were higher.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Another reason is that household sizes are getting smaller.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: More young married couples prefer a home of their own to living with their parents or extended families.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: At the same time, many prefer to live near their parents, so they can care for and support one another.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: More singles are also setting up homes of their own.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And more seniors now live alone or only with their spouse.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These trends mean we need more homes than we did in the past, as the total number of households has increased.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Many Members on both sides of this House have also called for the relaxation of eligibility criteria to provide wider access to public housing and shorter waiting times for Build-To-Order (BTO) flats.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But if we want more Singaporeans to qualify for HDB housing and to get their homes sooner, then we must build more homes and we must build them faster.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, the question, Mr Speaker, is not whether Singapore should continue to build homes, hospitals, schools and other developments to meet our people's needs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The question is where we build and how we build responsibly.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Let us go on next to where we build.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We first ask a series of practical questions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Can we make better use of existing land?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Can we build higher, go underground, bring compatible uses together, or better use under-utilised spaces?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: That is what we have been doing and we will continue to do.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For example, relocating Paya Lebar Air Base to Changi and Tengah will free up a substantial area for redevelopment, as will consolidating our port activities at Tuas Port.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We are also phasing out some golf courses and redeveloping older industrial areas for other uses.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We are already redeveloping the former Keppel Golf Course as part of the Greater Southern Waterfront.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This year, we announced Singapore's tallest public housing project – an over 60-storey development at Pearl's Hill.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Relaxing aviation height limits near airports also opens up new possibilities for us to build more intensely in suitable locations.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We are developing rock caverns at Gali Batu, building on earlier projects such as the Jurong Rock Caverns.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And through the North-South Corridor, we are moving vehicular traffic underground, freeing surface space for walking, cycling and greenery.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We are also doing more with existing sites and underused spaces, through integrated mixed-use developments, and by activating spaces beneath viaducts and on car park rooftops.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As we do all this, we pay close attention to greenery and heritage.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Today, Singapore has about 7,800 hectares of green spaces, including our nature reserves.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We are also strengthening ecological connections between core habitats.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: By 2030, we aim to restore and enhance 80 hectares of forest, marine and coastal habitats, and establish 300 kilometres of Nature Ways.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These efforts help make Singapore one of the world's greenest high-density cities.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Green View Index found that Singapore is ahead of most cities in urban tree coverage, including cities with much lower population densities.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We take a similar approach to heritage as well.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We have conserved more than 7,200 buildings and structures in over 100 areas.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Where possible, we retain significant heritage buildings and elements, and incorporate them into new developments.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Through our Master Plan, we engage Singaporeans and set out how we use our limited land for the next 10 to 15 years.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And we review the Master Plan every five years through a major public consultation exercise, to ensure it remains relevant to our nation's changing needs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: A site's zoning reflects its long-term planning intention.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But when we develop the site depends on our national needs, the availability of alternatives and if the supporting infrastructure is ready.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Within this framework, we will always do our best to retain sites with significant greenery and heritage value.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But there will be occasions when no other suitable site can meet the same need, in the same area and within the required timeframe.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And when that happens, we must weigh the trade-offs carefully and consider whether we can develop a site responsibly to meet an important national need, such as providing homes for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We proceed with great care when a site has significant ecological or heritage value.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Government agencies appoint independent external consultants to conduct an EIA or HIA, or both.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These studies draw on inputs from nature and heritage groups.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: First, they establish what is on the site today.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For an EIA, this means identifying the site's important habitats, plants, animals and ecological connections.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For a HIA, it means establishing the significance of the site's buildings, structures, landscape and other heritage attributes.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Second, the consultants assess how the proposed development could affect these features.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And third, they recommend how to avoid, reduce or mitigate potential impact to the site.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Depending on the site, this could mean retaining areas of high ecological significance, maintaining ecological corridors, preserving important buildings or incorporating heritage elements into the new development.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For an EIA, the consultants also propose a preliminary Environmental Management and Monitoring Plan (EMMP).

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The EMMP sets out mitigation measures, monitoring arrangements and reporting requirements that will apply during development.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, our general approach is to avoid impact where we can, reduce them where we cannot, and mitigate those that remain.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We publish the findings, potential impact and proposed mitigation measures in the EIA or HIA report.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This allows residents and the wider public to study the proposal and to give their feedback and views.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Agencies then consider the studies and feedback before finalising the detailed plans.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: EIAs and HIAs are not meant to justify a detailed plan that is already fixed.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: They are an integral part of the consultation process through which the plan is shaped.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Once development proceeds, HDB and the National Parks Board (NParks) will monitor the works and require contractors to provide regular updates, to ensure the measures are implemented properly.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For Gillman Barracks, we announced the intention to study the site for development during the 2024 Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The site was subsequently rezoned to reflect that intention under Master Plan 2025.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But we did not come to these sites first.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Over the years, we prioritised brownfield redevelopment in Clementi, Bukit Merah and surrounding areas.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In Clementi and Bukit Merah, we redeveloped several older estates under the Selective En bloc Redevelopment Scheme.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In Bukit Merah, we are redeveloping the former Keppel Golf Course, as I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But demand for housing in these estates remains strong.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Many Singaporeans, especially young families, want to continue living near their parents for mutual care and support.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Many understand this and so asked if we can build on sites that appear vacant or underused instead.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: One example is the former Raffles Junior College site at Mount Sinai where we are planning to introduce public housing in the near term, and the former bus facility at Ghim Moh where BTO construction is already in progress.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Some asked about the former Institute of Technical Education Headquarters site at the Dover-Medway area and a nearby site at Albert Winsemius Lane.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It will be considered for redevelopment in future after the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) line is completed.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For Gillman Barracks, some suggested building homes at Depot Lane Industrial Estate, the former Central Manpower Base (CMPB) and the "reserve site" at Pasir Panjang.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Depot Lane Industrial Estate is indeed part of our future housing supply and demolition of the buildings is currently ongoing to prepare the site.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: While the former CMPB has moved out of Depot Road camp, the site is still required by the Ministry of Defence and other users.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This also applies to the Pasir Panjang reserve site, where there are existing uses like the Ministry of Education Outdoor Adventure Learning Centre.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This site can only be redeveloped in the longer term.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In short, many of the sites suggested are already being developed for housing, are needed for other national purposes or cannot be redeveloped yet.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: That is why we need to develop Gillman Barracks and Sunset Way to meet our housing needs over the next decade.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But we recognise, Sir, that Gillman Barracks has both environmental and heritage value.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: That is why we commissioned the EIAs and HIA, because we assessed that the development could have significant environmental or heritage effects and wanted to carefully study the impact before finalising any plans.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These are comprehensive reports, reflecting months of data collection and analysis by independent experts.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We are also studying how to maintain ecological connections in the East-West and North-South directions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The East-West connection would link Telok Blangah Hill Park and HortPark, and the North-South connection would comprise an ecological corridor, supporting the movement of birds towards Berlayar Creek and Labrador Nature Reserve.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This would allow the future neighbourhood to build on the character and charm of the former colonial buildings.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But where a heritage building cannot be retained because of practical site constraints, we will explore other ways to preserve its history.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These include detailed documentation, salvaging and reusing suitable materials, and incorporating heritage interpretation into the future development.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This would preserve an important part of our railway heritage while maintaining ecological connectivity within the site.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We are also studying the retention of a natural stream and its surrounding riparian buffer, which provides refuge for wildlife.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These retained green areas will be supplemented with more native trees, and serving as buffers between the future neighbourhood and existing residential estates.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Our approach to both sites will be informed by science and evidence.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Gillman Barracks and Sunset Way lie within the wider Labrador Nature Park and Clementi Nature Corridor respectively, as NParks identified through its ecological profiling exercise.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The proposed retention areas are based on findings of the environmental studies, that aim to maintain ecological connectivity across these wider landscapes.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: HDB will also study how to design these future neighbourhoods to reduce urban heat.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This includes using environmental modelling to improve wind flow, incorporating greenery, using cool-paint and orientating residential blocks to minimise direct sun exposure.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We are not yet able to give an exact figure because the layout, scale and detailed design have not yet been finalised.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But in our current conceptual plan, we already reduced the number of homes to retain important green and heritage areas identified through the studies.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: If we conserve even more, we will build even fewer homes.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, we must weigh this trade-off carefully before reading a final decision.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: HDB has also been attending local grassroots advisers' dialogues with residents to hear their concerns and suggestions in person.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We appreciate the time and effort that many have put into studying the reports, attending dialogues and submitting detailed feedback.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I personally engaged many stakeholders myself and walked the ground at both Sunset Way and Gillman.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Young People's Action Party (PAP) and PAP Sustainability Group have also conducted engagements, gathering feedback and sharing that feedback with me and my team.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Some nature enthusiasts, heritage advocates and nearby residents also asked us to preserve more greenery and heritage.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: At the same time, we also heard from many Singaporeans, including residents in Clementi and Telok Blangah, about their desire for more affordable and accessible public housing.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Many tell us they hope their children will have an opportunity to live near them.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We will also publish a report summarising agencies' responses to the feedback and any amendments made to the original set of plans.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The challenge is how we balance these needs responsibly within our limited space.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We will and must always make the best use of existing land and safeguard our most important natural and heritage assets.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But there will be times where we cannot avoid difficult trade-offs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: When that happens, we must be clear about why we need to build, deliberate about where we build and take great care over how we build.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We must be honest with Singaporeans about the choices before us, listen carefully to their views and improve our plans wherever we can.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And after weighing all these different considerations, Government must decide in the best interests of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This is the approach we are taking for Gillman Barracks and Sunset Way.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We are studying the environmental and heritage findings, listening to public views and examining how the proposals can be improved before the detailed plans are finalised.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And they will continue to confront us as we build homes, strengthen our economy, expand our infrastructure and realise our vision of a City in Nature.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: They made them with courage and foresight, and Singapore is now better for it.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These came from in-person meetings, community sessions and written feedback, including well-researched proposals that the residents put together themselves.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I understand and appreciate the stated need for more housing and the potential benefits for many families.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Along these considerations, my residents have also raised deep concerns including the loss of biodiversity and ecological connectivity in the area, the loss of the very greenery that drew many residents to make this precinct to their home.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For many, Gillman Forest is a place of respite, reflection and connection.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Also raised is the impact on climate resilience and urban heat.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With that, I would like to ask four supplementary questions.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, can the Government clarify whether, and if so how, the earlier Berlayer EIA informed the Gillman Barracks EIA, particularly in relation to ecological connectivity corridor design and the cumulative impact across the two adjacent developments?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Residents have raised concerns over developing Berlayer and Gillman Barracks in close succession, particularly since both sides form part of the same ecological network and serve the same wildlife.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In this context, they have asked why the recommended ecological widths differ between the two, despite this shared ecology.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Gillman Forest links the Southern Ridges, which includes the Telok Blangah Hill Park, Berlayer Creek through to Labrador Nature Reserve and Kent Ridge Park, forming a larger ecological landscape.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Retaining it alongside shared residents, would also honour Singapore's 2021 pledge under the Glasgow Leaders' Declaration on Forests and Land Use to halt and reverse forest loss by 2030.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My second supplementary question: instead of residential development on Gillman Barracks, will the Government consider re-imagining and re-engineering the site to better meet the evolving needs of our next generation, creating spaces that protect and promote human creativity and connection?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My third supplementary question: will the Government review our planning and consultation processes to ensure they remain fit for purpose in the changing climate, specifically for forested or ecologically sensitive sites, could EIAs and public engagement begin at the master planning stage before land is slated for development?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My final supplementary question: will the Government provide a summary of the feedback collected, together with clarity on how it shaped the final development decisions?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This matters deeply to residents, who want assurance that their voices have made a difference.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: With regards to the Gillman EIA and its links to Berlayer, the Gillman EIA took into consideration the Berlayer Estate.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It has established an important connectivity, in fact, between Gillman and Berlayer for the movement of birds.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And these draw upon the findings from the NParks' ecological profiling exercise, which I mentioned earlier on, and the Keppel Club EIA.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And the conceptual plan, therefore proposes retaining the East-West Corridor, as I mentioned earlier on, and to establish a new North-South Corridor, to facilitate the movement of fauna.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, we acknowledge that there is ecological connectivity between sites, we have done that through the EIAs and the EIAs for each site is different because each site is unique, but where possible, we recognise the connectivity.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On building on new spaces within this site, as I have mentioned, we will take in those feedback in the consultation process, even beyond 6 August.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We will listen to residents and see where we can make adjustments.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, net-net, we are building a green city.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: All of these plans, be it in Sunset Way or Gillman, are meant to enhance that ecological connectivity and also to balance between development for homes, as well as green and heritage places.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have three supplementary questions for you today.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second supplementary question is, the Minister of State referred to quite a number of significant initiatives to free up further brownfield land, such as the relocation of Paya Lebar Air Base, the continuing relocation of our port terminals to Tuas, as well as taking back golf course land.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will enough of the brownfield land be freed up in time, so that we can continue to defer the development of green spaces like Maju Forest and Gillman Forest?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And my third supplementary question is regarding the location of the Cross Island Line Maju Station, does the Government regard the location of Maju Station as compelling or requiring the development of Maju Forest, in order to be able to sufficiently utilise the capacity that the station will provide?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: With regard to alternatives, I mentioned earlier on that we have looked in the vicinity of both Sunset Way as well as Gillman Barracks for alternative sites – vacant land, brownfield sites, underused sites.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And there are a variety of ways in which we consider the availability of the land, whether the land has leases remaining, whether they have additional uses, as I mentioned earlier on, whether the infrastructure surrounding that site is sufficient.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Because when you build homes for our people, you also need the surrounding infrastructure to support them.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Which brings me to Member's third point about train.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: When we look and select sites for homes for Singaporeans, it is not just on those considerations, but it is also very important for us to determine whether we can build amenities to support the community and housing, whether there is sufficient transport links including stations.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And when we do so, we do a couple of things.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And then, in the process, we get feedback and see how we can also better bring in amenities that will benefit home buyers and homeowners.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As planning principles, we know the first gives Singaporeans a stake in society and the second is really what continues to make us exceptional as nature is functional.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, how are these planning principles consistent, even through reviews of various Master Plans?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And can I confirm that MND is committed to the structured decision matrix and hierarchy, avoiding impact before minimising or mitigating in environmental or historical sites in guiding these decisions?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, our city in nature vision is ultimately about maintaining functional ecosystems that strengthen Singapore's resilience through biodiversity, ecological connectivity and climate adaptation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond the size of the green spaces which are retained, what ecological criteria does the Government use to determine if a site should be avoided altogether?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is there a desired minimum viability that we are optimising for longer term?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And when development does proceed, how does the Government monitor over time whether retained forests remain ecologically viable; for example, in terms of habitat quality, stormwater attenuation and urban cooling?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And finally, could the Minister of State please share more about the engagement process, including for this case of Maju Forest?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How does the Government ensure that development decisions are made consistently and transparently, specifically, which nature groups and experts are consulted, at what stages of planning and how does the feedback finally influence the planning outcome?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Has the Government considered whether EIAs and HIAs should be legislatively strengthened, brought earlier and the stages of the consultation process enshrined?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I explained earlier on our development process quite in detail.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And the developments that are assessed to have likely significant environmental and heritage impact are then subjected to the EIA and HIA process, which I mentioned earlier on.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And then, we work together with different stakeholders, community groups, residents, nature groups, to then study the EIA or HIA and to see where we can make adjustments.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On Member's point about the broader considerations, we have undertaken an ecological profiling exercise as I had mentioned, to better understand the role of sites in protecting and also supporting biodiversity and ecological connectivity.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These findings are important because they help to identify important habitats and ecological corridors.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It also helps us and guides planning on how to balance development with nature conservation.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But the development priorities and development projects that are close to sensitive areas will be subject to and in fact, are subject to greater scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And it guides measures to help us to mitigate the impact.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For example, we will protect our nature reserves and any nearby developments that may affect nature reserves are subject to very strict planning controls.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In consultation with the nature groups – I have met with many of them, including the Nature Society of Singapore, the Singapore Youth Voices for Biodiversity, LepakInSG, National University of Singapore academics and many residents as well.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As I mentioned earlier on, our consultation process will continue even after 6 August and we welcome more feedback and more views so that we can take in those, as we look to finalise our plans in later stage.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I take comfort in the fact that he mentioned that the plans have not been finalised and I take comfort in the good Minister of State's position that there has been an agreement to extend the consultation period, or at least the engagement post 6 August.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are good valuable explanations for the residents that I serve.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My questions arise out of possible alternative sites.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I accept the Government's national priority to have housing close to parents and to family – something that I support.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But I think we can look at alternative sites close to Maju Forest and here I have two: between the MSCP and the canal at Sunset Way there is currently a construction site for the Cross Island Line.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And if one was to build higher there, it would have beautiful waterfront living.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, that is one alternative that is within my own ward.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And pardon the pun, taking a leaf out of Dover Forest and the debate I had some years ago, we managed to find alternative housing sites that preserve half of Dover Forest – and it was a win-win situation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I invite the good Minister of State to look at this as a blank sheet of paper to see whether we can achieve such a win-win.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And therefore, an alternative site is also Clementi Avenue 5.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I understand that it is a worksite, a large worksite for the Cross Island Line, and it will be a rather eloquent and elegant position to put high rise HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I am not one to just throw the problem away.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the good Minister of State consider this?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The last point, Sir, if I may, arises out of Ms Sim Ann and my engagement on the ground.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have been responding to emails and we have visited Maju Forest twice.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And there is this great affinity for the forest, it is a part of their lives and there is also heritage.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, for all of these reasons, I ask for the same ethos, the same principles that governed the debate between the back bench and the front bench regarding Dover Forest, and if we can receive a win-win-win solution with alternative sites and as much mitigation as possible, I think that would be a great advantage and great fillip for this House.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I do support the national priority of building.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And if we can find a good win-win-win compromise.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: They have been very actively engaging myself, Minister Chee, Minister Indranee – very strongly speaking up on behalf of the residents at Sunset Way.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: They have conveyed many of the residents' feedback to us.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, they have been very actively engaged – both on the ground and to me, as well as our MND colleagues.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For example, the Albert Winsemius Lane site that he mentioned earlier near the MSCP is currently being used for LTA for the Cross Island Line.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, these are already measures that we have taken into consideration.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And we look into whether we can first use them.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Then, we see whether there are alternative sites for us to build.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, I thank Mr Christopher de Souza for his inputs and we urge him to continue engaging with us beyond 6 August, so that we can take in his residents' feedback and make relevant adjustments to the plans before they are finalised.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: One, in my Adjournment Motion on Serangoon River Forest earlier this year, I raised concerns that public engagement often takes place only after key land use directions, which includes non-consultative zoning decisions, have been determined.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: So, why were consultations not conducted before the scope and parameters of the environmental studies for Maju Forest and Gillman Barracks, for example, were established?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And will the Government consider engaging stakeholders at an earlier stage for future major redevelopment proposals?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: My next supplementary question: I would like to again urge the Minister of State to clarify whether the development plans for Gillman Barracks and the housing proposed under consideration remain open to substantive revision, and whether the Government is prepared to reduce development intensity or footprint, and consider alternative sites?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: What about the Protective Security Command at Ulu Pandan?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: My next supplementary question: would the Minister of State tell the House, what specific long-term population and household formation projections are driving the planning for HDB housing developments in Maju Forest and Gillman Barracks, and indeed elsewhere?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And will MND publish this figure so that the public can independently assess if clearing these forests is necessary now?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: My next supplementary question: given residents' concern about the loss of canopy cover, has HDB modelled the potential urban heat impact of the proposed developments on both sides and what measures are being considered to ensure surrounding neighbourhoods do not experience significant ambient temperature increases?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And finally, could I ask the Minister of State to consider extending the current one-month consultation period beyond 6 August, so that the residents, experts and civil society can have more time to review the reports and submit their feedback?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On the canopy cover and urban heat, I spoke about this in my main reply about how HDB is already taking these steps in existing and also future developments to reduce urban heat through many of these factors.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On population, I have also mentioned why currently, we require more housing.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Household sizes are smaller and there is increased demand for housing, particularly in the central areas where the two sites are.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And I also wanted to ask for Mr Dennis Tan and the Workers' Party (WP) colleagues in this House to also stand by us in this regard.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Because we have debated housing in this House many times.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We have debated it in, I think, 2023 on the debate on Motion for public housing and the WP stance on housing is very clear.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: First, Ms He Ting Ru, Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Louis Chua had proposed to reduce the age eligibility for singles to access public housing, from age 35 to 28.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Pritam Singh also suggested allowing a first-time couple who exceeded income eligibility criteria threshold to buy a BTO.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Louis Chua also pushed for the Government to increase public housing supply.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Louis Chua, in his Adjournment Motion in September 2022, implored the Government to take urgent and decisive steps to increase the availability of public housing and address the current demand-supply imbalance to ensure housing demand of all Singaporeans, not just singles, are met.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: He had also asked in the same Adjournment Motion for the Government to build residential homes ahead of demand and to have a fundamental rethink of the BTO system.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, all of these are very clear positions that housing is required and we need to build more.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And when we do that, it is not a question of why we build.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It is a question of where we build.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And in this case, we have been quite comprehensive in that regard.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On the public engagement, I also already mentioned that we will continue to engage the public, and we welcome public consultation and feedback beyond 6 August.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I ask Members to ask your questions, but not to ask the same questions in different ways for which Minister of State Tan has already answered.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But first, I do not think my Parliamentary Question was answered.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, (a) what is the threshold of harm that sets aside a site if a major negative EIA assessment does not?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And (b) whether under-used state land, including the grounds of black and white bungalows and ageing low-rise estates, had been assessed as an alternative?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I have been to the grounds of some of these black and white bungalows, and I think that they are very, very low density, and certainly, if you wanted to build more housing there, it would be ideal.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: First, residents value Telok Blangah for its greenery and forest, and that is a large part of its identity.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I think that removing the forest removes that identity.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, in the spirit of alternative sites, I think, could the car workshops around Alexandra Village Food Centre be considered for development?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Second, can there be a formal extension of the consultation deadline beyond 6 August?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Third supplementary question: many nature observers expressed to me deep disappointment in what they perceived to be the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment's (MSE's) lack of leadership and ownership in the decisions on Gillman Barracks and Maju Forest, and their perception that MSE has gone missing on this issue.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In this very year, 2026, that MSE has designated the "Year of Climate Adaptation", why has MSE not been seen leading and advocating for this forest?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Fu, I will come to you, after Minister of State Tan.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But with the EIA and the HIA, we have plans already to mitigate these possible impacts and we will do what we can to do so.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On alternative sites, we have already explained why and where; we have looked into alternative and brownfield sites.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And on the MSE, I disagree with his characterisation.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But at the end of the day, we will have to make decisions based on the best interest of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: You cannot say you want housing, as the WP has already mentioned multiple times and said in this House, but yet, then also in the same breath, say, "Why don't you do this?" and "Why don't you do that?" I think what is important is for us to look at the compatible uses, the trade-offs and for us to, at the same time, build homes for people whom both the WP and us want to build homes for and at the same time also preserve where possible heritage sites as well as ecological sites.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It requires us to make very deliberate decisions on where we build, which is alternative sites, and also how we build in this regard.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, I hope that the Member agrees with me, and I hope that he will work with us as well in engaging the nature groups, explain all of these different considerations.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And I also really wanted to say that MSE has been working very closely with us in terms of addressing many of these issues together.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For us, any one of us standing in front here, presenting a position to the Government, the rest of us are in support.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: So, I think if a WP Member is hoping for a fight between Ministers, I think they will be disappointed.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But in any case, the purpose of having the Year of Climate Adaptation is precisely for that: for all the agencies and the Ministries, when they are planning long-term land use, when they are planning long-term transport infrastructure, when they are planning long-term power infrastructure, to have a view on the adaptation that is needed, given the long-term climate change.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is not to change the way that we have worked effectively as a team in the Government.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: My fellow Young PAP advisors, Mr David Hoe and Ms Lee Hui Ying, heard two key concerns.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: They have been taught in school to make personal responsibility for sustainability but perceive a disconnect between this message and these developments.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: My first supplementary question: will the Ministry further enhance public accessibility of EIAs and HIAs, make them easier to understand among the general public?

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Second, our young accept that trade-offs are necessary, but they feel that they lack sufficient information to understand why this particular trade-off was made.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: It is also a very desirable site, given all the nature and the greenery surrounding it.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: How can we keep public housing at these sites affordable for HDB buyers?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And I understand that they will be engaging them further.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We can understand why our youths feel strongly about this and our youths ought to feel strongly about this.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These are important issues, these are important considerations.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It means they treasure our heritage and they treasure our green spaces.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We will continue to engage them beyond and to get their feedback on where we can make adjustments to the sites, but then also to explain the rationale as well.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On those sites, we are not yet able to give an exact figure about the plans because they are not finalised yet.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We could make, for example, potential adjustments to the layout, to the scale and to the detailed design.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I wanted to make the point that, where feasible, bungalows have been redeveloped or earmarked for future redevelopment already.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And previously, the demolished clusters, for example, of bungalows at Seletar Camp have made way for an industrial park – and that supports our aerospace sector.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, again, it reinforces our point that, where we can, we will prioritise brownfield sites and vacant sites, but where we cannot, then when we have to build, then we build very carefully, taking into account the EIA, the HIA, and then also looking at mitigation measures, working together with residents, communities, youth groups, nature groups and the like.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: But since then, Maju Forest has become ecologically significant amidst the loss of many other green spaces in Singapore, including Tengah and parts of Bukit Brown.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The Minister of State has mentioned that MND has safeguarded a lot of green spaces, but there are also different types of green spaces.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Destroying a secondary forest and then replacing it with a park yields the same amount of green space, but the ecological impact is completely different.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: So, in light of this, will the Government consider reclassifying forested greenfield sites that are currently zoned for development into sites to be preserved wherever feasible?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: And if not, what factors might lead the Ministry to consider re-zoning forested greenfield sites that have already been identified for development, for park or nature reserve use?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: A second question is, what is the threshold for conducting EIAs before developments on greenfield sites?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And I appreciate Members of this House for conveying those concerns of their residents as well as the community, in this regard.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It is important to ask these questions and it is on the Government to explain them, to explain the different aspects of it and to also ask for the public as well as residents to work with us in the design of these areas.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I have answered quite substantively, the questions that the Member had asked, particularly the ones that I had answered Ms Nadia Samdin, about how we look at the overall green space, the ecological profiling exercise.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I have also answered before, how we look at alternative sites; and I also answered earlier on, how the EIA and HIA is meant to identify where their ecological and heritage significance and then, where, that is, what is today, how the proposed development may impact ecological and heritage features within the site and also, how we also mitigate the impact.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: If we look at sites like, even Maju, in 1976, it was a brownfield site.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The vegetation started growing there and then, of course, right now, even as we plan for Sunset Way, we factor in those green features.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The stream, for example; the ecological corridor, for example; the old Jurong line, for example.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But there are there now, they have grown onto an original brownfield site.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And when we plan, we already factor in that because we want to preserve these green sites and these green features, we already are lowering the number of homes that we can build on these sites.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, we take those into consideration and we will be able to build desirable homes for our people living close to their parents and also, enjoy the greenery that abuts these sites.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Would the Ministry consider publishing a forward-looking list of intended planning studies within the near term, say about two to three years, that may affect areas with heritage or ecological significance, and actively engage the community from the outset?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The second supplementary question will be, would the Ministry consider incorporating measures of non-market values, including existence value, bequest value and cultural value, into its evaluation framework for redevelopment decisions affecting heritage or natural areas?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Again, I had mentioned earlier on, how we look at the overall landscape as well as our island and how we have undertaken, for example, ecological profiling exercises, to better understand the role of sites in supporting, for example, biodiversity and ecological connectivity.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: All of these, in concert, these findings do help us.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: They help us to identify important habitats and ecological corridors to guide how we plan and how we can balance development with nature conservation.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As part of this planning approval process, and I had answered that earlier on as well, all development proposals are screened for potential ecological and heritage impact before we proceed.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And the developments that are assessed to likely have high significant ecological and heritage impact are then subject to the EIA, and again, I have mentioned how we do that as well.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, I would like to respond to the Minister of State.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I am not sure I agree that his characterisation of the WP's position is a fair one.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I think the question at hand here is not about whether or not we should build more.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The question is and I believe that Members of this House are actually asking whether this location and the decisions, or at least the announcements have been made, are going to be the best given that there is a lot of pressure on housing.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We all know that residents have balloted many, many, many times for housing.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, again, we are not disagreeing about about this, but the question before us today is whether or not these sites are the best places to build.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And we also want to understand a bit more from the Government, why these announcements have been made, what are the considerations that have gone into it?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In this regard, I also want to ask a couple of supplementary questions on this.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I also noticed that Minister Chee earlier in the last few days also mentioned that HDB is continuing to study the impact of reducing BTO age, and I am just curious about whether or not the announcement of the development of these two areas is tied in any way to any potential reduction in BTO eligibility ages?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The last supplementary question that I would like to ask is whether or not, we have heard a lot about EIAs and HIAs and when these are being conducted.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We also heard a bit about zoning, and the Minister of State mentioned earlier that Sunset Way has been zoned since 1980 for residential housing purposes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, I just wanted to know whether or not, whether there had been any precedence where formal EIAs or HIAs have been conducted before any zoning changes or zoning decisions are made in order for us to have a bit more forward guidance in deciding to do a formal assessment, something a bit more formalised – EIAs or HIAs – before we even decide to change the zoning.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And she also acknowledged that there is a lot of pressure on housing.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: She mentioned earlier on that residents coming and balloting many times for housing.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I am sure she faced that with her residents coming to her.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, there is a huge demand for housing.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And the question then, as Ms He mentioned, is whether the alternative sites, whether we have sufficiently looked at alternatives.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But these are all considerations that I have already mentioned.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On the BTO eligibility age, Minister Chee had mentioned that we are reviewing that.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Then on the EIA and the HIA, I think there has been a little bit of misunderstanding on this.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We need an EIA and HIA to present a proposal and that proposal then, is meant for agencies, it is meant for the community, it is meant for residents to then look at the proposal, see where the impact is and see how to mitigate that impact.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The EIAs are naturally very extensive, they run over 300 pages long.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But we also have executive summaries of it.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And with these engagements then, we can also go into the detail.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, the engagements, for example, that Mr Christopher de Sousa and Minister Sim Ann or Miss Rachel Ong has organised; or many others outside of it; or the YP has organised.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These go into the details, make it a little bit easier.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And the EIA and the HIA are plans.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It showcases what is there, where the impact would be and also where the potential mitigations are.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And again, as I reiterated, the consultation and the feedback process is ongoing and we hope that many will continue to give us that feedback.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We will make the changes as necessary, because the development plans are not final.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We spent over 70 minutes on this issue.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: One from Eileen Chong and one from Joan Pereira.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have two supplementary questions and one clarification for the Minister of State.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister of State spoke about the better use of existing land, building taller where we can and using under-utilised land.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, in this regard, I also note that the Government has committed to the Voluntary Early Redevelopment Scheme (VERS) from early 2030 to renew ageing estates.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I would like to ask, when the recommendation was made to clear parts of Maju Forest, Gillman Forest and Gillman Barracks for housing, was there any consideration to bring forward this renewal as an alternative?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My second supplementary question is actually related to the Minister of State's earlier reply about how he was unable to share the exact housing yield of these sites, because the layouts have not been finalised.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I would like to ask whether there is a target per site yield that HDB is looking at?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I note in the 2025 draft URA Master Plan that it does contain indicative site yields for sites, like Newton, 5,000; the Patterson, 1,000; and also for Bayshore, 10,000 to 12,000, and so forth.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But none has been given in this Master Plan for Maju Forest as well as for the Gillman Barracks sites.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And related to this, I would like to ask the Minister of State, what is the exact size of the housing demand that these sites are meant to respond to?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is something that my colleague Dennis Tan has asked.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How much of this housing demand reflects local family formation per the Minister of State's outline about households getting smaller versus planned population growth?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given the volume of questions raised in this House today and the clear public interest and feedback on this, could the Minister of State clarify whether MND will be extending the consultation window beyond 6 August —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Well, that has been answered three times, if I recall rightly.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: Just a clarification: whether this window is extended beyond 6 August, just like what was done for Dover Forest in 2021, or is it simply that MND will continue to engage the public and relevant agencies beyond 6 August?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: I am asking this so that Singaporeans can have more of a meaningful opportunity to participate.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: That is why we are extending that, so that we can make adjustments.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On VERS, this is a long-term policy to have gradual redevelopment.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But earlier on, I have already mentioned why there is a demand for housing.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I have already mentioned the smaller household sizes, I have mentioned greater family formation and also where people want homes.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, that is why we need to take this decision, look at the sites, look at where to build, look at alternatives and then, where we build, we do our best to mitigate the impacts of development – all to build homes for Singaporeans, which is our main objective.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have a supplementary question for the Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: SLA has also kept the tenants updated on the environmental and heritage studies which I mentioned earlier on, as well as upcoming development works.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For arts tenants, I thank Ms Joan Pereira for thinking of our arts practitioners in the site.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I want to assure her that SLA is working closely with the National Arts Council (NAC) to support them.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: NAC will continue to engage the tenants and work with relevant agencies to facilitate their relocation, where possible, including pointing them to suitable alternative spaces and opportunities within Singapore's arts ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And it really reflects upon all Members of the House reflecting the voices of our people, reflecting the voices of youths, reflecting the voices of our residents, reflecting the voices of our communities.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Because we should care, our children should care, our youths should care.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: That they care enough to come together, to write to us, to ask tough questions, but also to walk with us and to work with us to find solutions together to build homes, to also protect our precious green and heritage spaces.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We can build homes that are nestled in greenery.
